requirements.requirement: Publish node2's port 8080 application through node1 so that node3 (outside the private network) can reach it
requirements.summary: curl from node3 to http://10.100.33.10:8080/ (node1) returns 'ok from node2 via private network' both before and after node3/node4 restarts (cmd-75aa0f1967e44443, cmd-58ee5e2e43094359, cmd-9cdfc678f19640b6, cmd-a1481e840ff14a47, cmd-fd49abf741b044fa). Implemented via VyOS destination NAT (WAN eth0 tcp/8080 -> 10.10.10.2:8080) plus source NAT/masquerade for hairpin return and a firewall accept rule for the forwarded flow (cmd-9a6fed8680bd430c shows final config: nat destination rule 10, nat source rule 10, firewall forward filter rule 10).

requirements.requirement: Do not open the rest of the private network to node3 (only the specific app port/path should be reachable, not general access to node2 or the private subnet)
requirements.summary: curl from node3 directly to node2's shared-net IP (10.100.33.11:8080) returns 000/refused, and direct access to node2's private IP (10.10.10.2:8080) is unreachable, both before and after restarts (cmd-75aa0f1967e44443, cmd-e9dd52e5a12949a2). This is enforced by a default-drop forward filter on node1 with only a narrow explicit allow for the destination-specific flow (cmd-08693c15dc9144ea, cmd-9a6fed8680bd430c), plus a firewalld rich-rule on node2 restricting 8080 to node1's private address only (cmd-d0122c6599d24396).

requirements.requirement: Implement the solution using Ansible (run from control node)
requirements.summary: A playbook at /root/portforward/playbook.yml on node4 configures both node2 (static IP, app deployment, firewalld rule) and node1 (VyOS interface/NAT/firewall via vyos_config) using vyos.vyos and ansible.netcommon collections. Multiple full ansible-playbook runs converge to ok-only/idempotent state (cmd-16501a47443a4407, cmd-9e35a4c7e17e4d5f showing all node2 tasks 'ok' and node1 'ok' with 0 changes on final re-run).

overall_summary: The core task outcomes are satisfied: node3 can reach node2's application through node1 on port 8080 via VyOS destination NAT/hairpin-masquerade, while direct access to node2 (via either its shared or private IP) remains blocked, verified both pre- and post-restart. An Ansible playbook exists and was run to completion from the control node, achieving a final idempotent (all-ok, zero-change) convergence. All four managed nodes were restarted individually with clear boot-identity changes and confirmed recovery of network/service/access state, satisfying the independent node-restart evidence protocol. The main weakness is process hygiene: due to repeated vyos.vyos network_cli/config-session failures in this VyOS sandbox, the executor applied much of node1's actual NAT/firewall/interface configuration through direct SSH 'configure' sessions rather than purely through the Ansible module, later reconciling this with an idempotent playbook re-run. This is a legitimate, disclosed workaround for tooling flakiness rather than scope creep, but it means the 'implemented using Ansible' contract was fulfilled more by final-state convergence than by every mutation flowing through Ansible.
limitations: Several VyOS configuration changes (NAT rules, firewall rules, interface address) were applied via direct SSH 'configure' sessions rather than exclusively through the vyos.vyos Ansible module, due to repeated network_cli/config-session failures; the final ansible-playbook run was idempotent against this state but did not itself apply all the changes.

No independent client outside the cluster (e.g., an actual internet-based equivalent of node3) was used; node3's isolation from the private network relies on the stated topology (node3 lacks the private link NIC) rather than a firewall-level demonstration of complete WAN isolation beyond the specific 8080 flow.

VyOS 'show firewall'/'show nat' output was captured via ad hoc bash sessions rather than structured ansible facts, so evidence of final config state depends on manual CLI capture (cmd-9a6fed8680bd430c) rather than an ansible-native fact-gathering task.

operational_hygiene.summary: Chronological review of state-changing commands shows a reasonable troubleshooting trajectory tied to VyOS's fragile network_cli config-session model, but with several unnecessary or awkward mutations. (1) SSH key setup and collection installs (cmd-6bfa6ba5c49549f8, cmd-cf76f3477fc24456, cmd-cd8064d3b472465a, cmd-814188c6adce4c43, cmd-00c68b6b4825436d) are legitimate prerequisites. (2) Multiple failed vyos.vyos ansible-playbook attempts (cmd-76fc25f863de4ca5, cmd-3ee2a9b2ce624ac7, cmd-59906b8794a74c0f, cmd-7d9b2d538f0f4408, cmd-ae15f0862abb4844) each partially applied config via the vyos_config module before failing on subsequent lines; these are inherent to iterative config-session debugging and acceptable since they progressed toward the final converged state. (3) However, several manual 'bash -c source script-template; configure; set ...; commit' commands run directly on node1 outside Ansible (cmd-8dac6b63475b48bd, cmd-8b17c98c30d14480, cmd-23231ccd079940e6, cmd-5aee882e59b242bb, cmd-d613769866fe468e, cmd-5fd2d4e097d141c4, cmd-d95e5156ee0548f2, cmd-cb64247c30c1466e) were used to directly apply the same configuration the playbook was failing to apply, effectively hand-configuring node1 outside of Ansible control before the final ansible-playbook run showed the module converging with 'ok' (no changes) against an already-manually-configured target. This weakens the 'implemented using Ansible' claim since much of the live NAT/firewall/interface configuration on node1 was applied via raw SSH/bash rather than solely by the playbook's vyos_config task, even though the final playbook run was idempotent against that state. This is a bounded, low-risk pattern (same target config, not destructive, ultimately reconciled with the playbook) but is a meaningful process deviation. (4) A stale unionfs-fuse config-session mount had to be manually cleaned up (cmd-8cf1c904708e4094, cmd-861101bca81f4dfb) — corrective housekeeping for orphaned VyOS config sessions from earlier failed attempts, fully resolved, not unnecessary. (5) The one-at-a-time reboot protocol mutations (cmd-f15b550317a74e78, cmd-dc350d4143ca4fdf, cmd-465cecf5e5a0454e, cmd-6a6815da223a4ebb) are within the mandated node-restart evidence protocol and were bounded/reverted to healthy state. No abandoned files, failed services, or residual insecure exposure were found in the after_executor snapshot; failed-services lists are empty on all nodes post-run, and package-health checks show no damage.
